papers.title: Replicating chaotic dynamics from sparse sensors with recurrent latent states
papers.abstract: Forecasting a high-dimensional nonlinear system from a few point sensors requires an estimate of the current state and a model of its evolution. Reduced-order models usually take the full state as input, so with only sparse sensors they require an auxiliary full-state estimate whose error is inherited by the latent representation. We instead build the latent state from sensor measurements alone, using a shallow recurrent decoder (SHRED) network that encodes a history of point measurements, and train an echo state network to advance that latent state autonomously. We show that the resulting latent dynamics replicate the long-term dynamical invariants of the underlying system rather than merely tracking its short-term trajectory. For the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the autonomous latent model reproduces the leading Lyapunov exponents of the full system from 25 of 128 state components, using a latent state with 6-14% as many components as the full state. Because Lyapunov exponents are invariant under smooth coordinate changes, this is consistent with the recurrent encoder recovering an embedding of the attractor, in the spirit of Takens' delay embedding theorem. The recurrent encoding also decouples forecast skill from reconstruction accuracy. SHRED reconstructs less accurately than a convolutional autoencoder given the full state, yet it forecasts comparably on the simpler chaotic case and better on the more complex one. For Kolmogorov flow, with sensors at 6% of grid points and a latent state 0.3% the size of the vorticity field, the autonomous model remains on the learned latent manifold over long horizons.

papers.title: Construction of a Deployable Hard-Constrained Turbulence Closure
papers.abstract: We present a framework for constructing deployable hard-constrained turbulence closures of unclosed terms in the transport equations of Reynolds stresses and turbulent dissipation rate. The framework is built from modules, each performing a single task. The closure module represents the closure with a small network, while the state module represents the flow state during training. The closure network is coupled to the state network through the governing equation residuals, allowing the closure to be learned without reference closure values being supplied as training data. The coordinate module learns monotone input coordinates that help both networks resolve sharp changes. Within the network architecture, the boundary condition (BC) module imposes boundary values exactly using the Theory of Functional Connections, and the realizability module keeps the closure realizable. We apply the framework to decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) with experimental and direct numerical simulation trajectories. Here, the state module is a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), the BC module imposes the initial state and the closure's low and high Reynolds number limits, and the realizability module ensures growth of the Taylor microscale. Across ten random seeds, the framework reduces root-mean-square seed-to-seed closure variation by about 95\% relative to the unconstrained model over the training and held-out range. The deployed 18-parameter closure network requires only the Taylor scale Reynolds number and can be exported as a standalone C function.

papers.title: Flip rate prediction in the double pendulum
papers.abstract: The intermediate-energy double pendulum is a prototypical chaotic system. Despite its irregular motion, it exhibits recurrent flips--events in which one of the arms passes over the top. We develop a statistical prediction for the mean flip rate in terms of phase-space flux. Applying this flux-based approach to the equal-mass, equal-arm ("egalitarian") double pendulum, we find excellent agreement between the statistical prediction and numerical simulations: ensemble-averaged flip rates agree to within 1%, while even the statistics of individual chaotic trajectories agree at the few-percent level, quantifying the validity of the ergodic approximation. This agreement holds for flips of either arm and over a broad range of energies. This flux-based approach is closely related to that used for the egalitarian three-body system. A central role is played by the saddle orbits: periodic orbits that tend to the periodic saddle eigenmode as the energy approaches the saddle energy from above and approximately follow the ridge of the potential at higher energies. These orbits provide a natural dividing surface for defining flips while avoiding recrossings. Indeed, the resulting distribution of crossing times exhibits a distinct gap. It is argued that the corresponding flux-over-a-saddle prediction provides a preferred realization of the flux-based approach. We also present two simplified alternative dividing surfaces, including one based on a remarkably accurate analytic approximation to the saddle orbits, and show that both yield statistical predictions in agreement with the corresponding simulated rates.

papers.title: The Chaotic Dynamics of Coupled Maps with Convection and Diffusion
papers.abstract: We explore the fundamental role of convective and diffusive coupling on the spatiotemporal chaos of a large one-dimensional lattice of coupled maps on a ring. Extensively chaotic dynamics persist over nearly the entire range of spatial coupling strengths that yield numerically stable dynamics. The spatial coupling affects the shape of the spectrum of Lyapunov exponents, for increasing convective coupling the leading Lyapunov exponents increase while the large negative Lyapunov exponents decrease resulting in a significant increase in the fractal dimension of the dynamics. Convective coupling increases the localization of the leading Lyapunov vector and adds significant power to the high-wavenumber components of the spectrum of covariant Lyapunov vectors while increasing their entanglement. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the diffusive coupling matrix remain insightful quantities in the presence of nonlinear convective coupling. We discuss the implications of these findings for high-dimensional chaotic dynamics of large transport systems.

papers.title: Linking Dynamical Time Scales and Experimental Design to Parameter Identifiability from Time-Series Observations
papers.abstract: Parameter estimation in chaotic models often relies on prescribed summary statistics, whose ability to constrain parameters may be difficult to establish in advance. Different parameters influence different features and time scales of the dynamics, so the record length and sampling interval needed to constrain them may differ. We choose to learn a representation directly from the trajectory and use it as our summary statistic. The recurrent encoder that produces this representation is trained jointly with a conditional normalizing flow for amortized posterior estimation. We use the Lorenz-63 and two-scale Lorenz-96 systems to investigate how inference depends on the observed variables, record length and sampling interval, and compare our results with the state-of-the-art Calibrate--Emulate--Sample method. In Lorenz-96, learned summaries of a 2 model-time-unit (MTU) record achieve estimation skill comparable to prescribed second-moment statistics from substantially longer records for several parameters. Fast-process parameters remain weakly constrained by slow-variable records across the tested 2 to 100 MTU windows, while adding fast-field averages improves their recovery from 2 MTU. Coarser sampling weakens inference from fast-field observations, but longer coverage can partly compensate. Once trained for a given observation setting, the estimator we develop returns posteriors for compatible records without further model integration. These proof-of-concept results illustrate how data-driven learning of summaries can be used to inform the design of observations in dynamical systems.

papers.title: Relative periodic orbits of a free spinning loop
papers.abstract: A closed elastic string with no external forces can hold any shape while its material moves steadily along the curve (a steady axial motion), because its tension and the force needed to turn the material around a bend are both proportional to the curvature. I compute the periodic motions that grow from the simplest of these motions, the spinning ring, by Newton's method on a chain of masses. They include rotating waves that turn at twice the rotation rate of the material, standing "flappers" with two to five lobes, and period-doubled and period-tripled orbits. The chain only approximates the string. The orbits and their strong instabilities change little with more masses and are properties of the continuous string. Most weak instabilities change with the number of masses and are artifacts of approximating the string by a finite chain. The saddle flapper of a loop stretched 30% beyond its natural length is neutrally stable at small heights and unstable at large ones. An unstable saddle flapper trades energy back and forth with an in-plane oval, and at large amplitude the energy spreads to the shortest waves of the chain. For Keller's linear string, whose tension is proportional to the stretched length, every motion is periodic, and every knot carries an exactly periodic flapper. For a Hookean string the curvature of a knot couples a ripple to stretching waves that travel at a different speed, and in the simulations a ripple on a sliding knot does not return to its starting shape. Whether a Hookean knot carries any periodic flapper is open.
